```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "#>")
library(metacheck)
```

When authors share their data and analysis code, the idea is that anyone should be able to run that code on that data and get the results reported in the paper. But sharing data and code in a way that results are reproducible is difficult, and researchers have often not received training in how to share data and code. As a consequence, there are often basic mistakes in public repositories that stand in the way of computationally reproducible results. Automated checks can help researchers identify and fix these mistakes, such as not sharing all files that are loaded in code, using absolute instead of relative filepaths, using values that are not computed in the code that is shared, changing file names so they no longer match the code, or not loading all libraries. 

Checking whether data and code is reproducible is tedious. It also often requires repeated back and forths between the person performing the checks, and the researchers sharing data and code. Ideally, checks do not just focus on whether code runs, but also whether all results in a manuscript are reproduced by the code, but this takes a lot of time. 

Metacheck's `reproducibility_check` module attempts to perform all these checks automatically. When it succeeds, researchers and/or reviewers, data managers, or editors know that data and code is shared in a reproducible manner, and they do not need to perform manual checks. This saves everyone time, and leads to data and code repositories that are more useful for science. Our reproducibility check module is completely code-based. It uses no AI (although modules it builds on, such as `data_check`, can optionally use a large language model, by setting `llm_use(TRUE)`, to better understand the files in a repository, such as which files belong to which study), and it can run locally on your computer without sending information to an external server.

This chapter starts with the module at work on two versions of the same small study: one where every reported result can be reproduced, and one where several cannot. The sections after the example describe each step of the check in detail.

## Computationally reproducing a simple Stroop experiment

Both papers analyse the same classroom data from Daniël Lakens's introduction to psychology and technology course. Students named the ink color of words that matched the color (the word "red" printed in red) and of words that did not (the word "red" printed in green), and reported the time they needed in seconds. Both papers report four results: the mean and standard deviation of the reaction times in each condition, the correlation between the reaction times in the two conditions, a paired *t*-test for the Stroop effect, and a comparison of the Stroop effect between the students tested in 2013 and in 2014.

- The **good** paper, <https://github.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper>, computes every reported number in its analysis code. The manuscript is a Quarto document, so the text prints these numbers directly from the analysis.
- The **bad** paper, <https://github.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper_bad>, has several common mistakes deliberately built in. The results were typed into the text by hand, the shared data contain a value the authors removed before their own analysis without saying so, some reported results are not computed by the code at all, and the code stops with an error before it reaches the last analysis.

## Running the code locally, or using our server on SURF

The reproducibility check runs code that other people wrote. That is not without risk. A script can delete files, read files that have nothing to do with the project, or send information over the internet, by accident or on purpose. By default, `execute = TRUE` runs each script in a separate R process on your own computer. This prevents a script that crashes from taking your own R session down with it, but the script can still reach every file on your computer, and the internet. That is fine for the two repositories in this chapter, which we made ourselves, but not for code from a repository you have not created, as a bad actor might insert problematic code.

For such code, add `sandbox = "docker"`. [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) is a program that runs software in a *container*: a closed environment on your computer, separated from the rest of the system. Metacheck runs every script in its own container, and has set up these containers so that the code can do as little harm as possible:

- The container has no internet connection while the code runs. Only the step before it, which installs the packages the code needs, is connected to the internet, and in that step none of the paper's own code runs.
- The code runs on a copy of the repository's files, in a temporary folder. That folder is the only place on your computer it can write to, and the files on the rest of your computer are not visible inside the container.
- The code runs as an ordinary user without administrator rights, cannot obtain extra rights, and can start only a limited number of processes.
- Each script is stopped after a time limit, 10 minutes by default.

No sandbox makes running unknown code completely safe: a flaw in Docker itself could in principle still be exploited. But these settings close off the usual ways in which a script can do damage. [Two ways to run the code](#two-ways-to-run-the-code) below lists the exact settings, and compares them with running code without Docker.

Running the check in Docker takes some preparation, and disk space. You need Docker Desktop (on Windows and macOS) or Docker Engine (on Linux), and the space Docker Desktop itself needs. The first time you run the check, Docker downloads Metacheck's image for R code: R, Quarto, and the roughly 750 R packages that occurred in a scan of thousands of R files shared with psychology papers, together about 4.9 GB. Python code runs in a second image of about 2.7 GB. Because most packages a paper needs are already in the image, they do not have to be installed again for every paper, which makes the check much faster (but at the expense of a large docker image that you install once). [The pre-built Docker image](#the-pre-built-docker-image-and-why-it-exists) below explains how it was built.

If you do not use R, the [Docker installation](get-started.qmd#docker-installation) runs Metacheck's website on your own computer, with the same checks. It needs about 1.7 GB of disk space and a computer with 8 GB of memory, plus Docker. There, the code of a repository runs inside Metacheck's own container: it cannot reach the files on your computer, but unlike in the sandbox described above, it can use the internet. The packages the code needs are downloaded while the check runs. Running the check on your own computer also means that an unpublished manuscript never leaves it, which matters for editors and reviewers who may not upload a submission to an external server.

The easiest way to try the check is our server on SURF Research Cloud, which runs on the servers of SURF, the cooperative of the Dutch universities, in the Netherlands. You need nothing but a web browser. On [Metacheck's website](https://metacheckserve.metacheck.src.surf-hosted.nl/), upload a PDF under *Run Metacheck on a Paper* and tick *Also run the code in the paper's repository*, or, under *Run Metacheck on a Repository*, choose a folder or a .zip file, or paste a link to an online repository such as GitHub or OSF; there, running the code is ticked by default. The [ResearchBox Check](https://metacheckserve.metacheck.src.surf-hosted.nl/researchbox/) and the [TU/e Data Manager Check](https://metacheckserve.metacheck.src.surf-hosted.nl/datamanager/) run the check too. The server already has the most common R and Python packages. It first installs any other packages the code needs from CRAN or PyPI, but not packages from GitHub or other links, and then runs each script for at most 5 minutes, in a closed sandbox without internet access. Uploaded files are deleted as soon as they have been read, and the report is kept on the server for one hour, so save it if you want to keep it.

The server's capacity is shared by everyone who uses it, so it is meant for checking a paper or a repository now and then. If you want to check many papers, run Metacheck on your own computer, or [build your own server on SURF Research Cloud](get-started.qmd#your-own-server-on-surf-research-cloud), which researchers at Dutch institutions can do through their institution or with a free NWO grant. The [Setting up Metacheck](get-started.qmd) chapter describes all these options.

## Running the check in R

We illustrate the module in R. Metacheck reads a paper from its PDF. We download both PDFs from GitHub, and `convert()` turns each into a structured file that `read()` loads into R. If you want to follow along in the Metacheck website, download the two papers from [here](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper/main/output/analysis.pdf) and [here](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper_bad/main/analysis.pdf). 

```{r}
#| eval: false
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper/main/output/analysis.pdf",
  destfile = "good_paper.pdf", mode = "wb"
)
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper_bad/main/analysis.pdf",
  destfile = "bad_paper.pdf", mode = "wb"
)
paper <- read(convert(file_path = "good_paper.pdf", save_path = "."))
bad_paper <- read(convert(file_path = "bad_paper.pdf", save_path = "."))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# a local copy of the converted papers is used here, so this page does not
# depend on the conversion server when it is built
paper <- read("../converted/good_paper.json")
bad_paper <- read("../converted/bad_paper.json")
```

Both papers link to their repository. The [repo_check](mod-repo-check.qmd) module in Metacheck supports over 270 data repositories, and can automatically download files from these repositories.

Running the module is a single line. By default, `reproducibility_check` only inspects the code without running it. `execute = TRUE` is needed to actually run the full computational reproducibility check:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
mo_good <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check", execute = TRUE)
mo_good$traffic_light
```

```{r}
cat(mo_good$summary_text)
```

The light is green: every script ran without an error, and every result reported in the manuscript was among the results the code produced when it ran. `mo_good$table` lists each script and what happened when it was run:

```{r}
mo_good$table[, c("file_name", "outcome")]
```

`clean_data.R` turns the raw data file into the processed data file, and `analysis.qmd` is the manuscript, whose code chunks contain the analysis. The repository also contains `renv/activate.R`, a script the `renv` package adds to a project to set up its package library. The module does not check the contents of this folder, because it knows it is not part of the analysis.

`mo_good$match_table` shows, for each result reported in the paper, whether it was found in the output of the code, and in which analysis:

```{r}
mo_good$match_table[, c("reported", "found", "confidence", "analysis")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

A result is not compared as single numbers, but as a whole: the *t*-value, the degrees of freedom, and the *p*-value of one test have to appear together in the output of one analysis. Any single number will sooner or later turn up somewhere in a large output by coincidence, but several numbers of one test appearing together in one analysis will not.

::: callout-tip
## Making your own results findable

The module can only find a result if the code produces it while it runs, in a form the module recognises. In the good paper, every reported number is computed in a code chunk, and the text of the manuscript only rounds these values. A number that is computed only inside the text, by an inline R expression in Quarto or R Markdown, is not part of the code that is run, so it cannot be found.

The module recognises the results of test functions such as `t.test()` and `cor.test()`, of summaries such as `sapply(stroop_data[, c("congruent", "incongruent")], mean)`, and of effect sizes from the `effectsize` package, also when they are stored in a variable (`ttest_result <- t.test(...)`). A number computed by hand, such as a Cohen's *d* computed as `mean(diff) / sd(diff)`, is found when the code prints it, but not when it is only stored in a variable.
:::

A green light means that the numbers in the paper follow from the shared code and data. It does not mean that the analysis was the right one to perform.

Now let's see what the module returns if we run it on the bad paper:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
mo_bad <- module_run(bad_paper, "reproducibility_check", execute = TRUE)
mo_bad$traffic_light
```

```{r}
cat(mo_bad$summary_text)
```

The light is red, because the analysis code stopped with an error:

```{r}
mo_bad$table[, c("file_name", "outcome")]
cat(mo_bad$run_results$error)
```

The code compares the Stroop effect between the two years using a column `stroop_effect`, but no line of the code creates that column. The authors presumably created it in their R console while they worked, so the code ran on their own computer, but it cannot run for anyone else. This is one of the most common reasons shared code fails.

Before the code was run, the module also changed one line of it. `mo_bad$modifications` lists every change:

```{r}
mods <- mo_bad$modifications
mods[mods$change_type == "setwd_removed", c("change_type", "detail")]
```

The code starts with `setwd("C:/Users/dlakens/Desktop/stroop_study")`, which sets the folder R works in to a folder that only exists on the author's computer. The module skips this line, and reports that it did, because it would stop the code on any other computer.

Now the comparison between the paper and the output:

```{r}
mo_bad$match_table[, c("reported", "found", "confidence", "analysis")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Only the mean and standard deviation of the congruent condition were found. Each of the other results is missing for a different reason:

- **The incongruent mean and standard deviation** (*M* = 23.0, *SD* = 4.78) are not in the output. The output contains the statistics the code did compute:

  ```{r}
  mo_bad$stat_output[[1]]$long[, c("analysis", "statistic", "value")]
  ```

  The incongruent mean is 22.08, with a standard deviation of 11.64. The reason is in the data. One participant has a reaction time of -99 in the incongruent condition:

  ```{r}
  bad_data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper_bad/main/stroop.csv")
  summary(bad_data$Incongruent)
  ```

  -99 is a code for a missing value, not a reaction time. The authors removed this participant before computing the results in their paper, but the code they shared does not, so it analyses -99 as if it were a reaction time.
- **The paired *t*-test**, *t*(130) = 18.04, is not found for the same reason: the shared code analyses all 132 participants, including the -99, and gets *t*(131) = 6.77. The reported *p* = .25 and Cohen's *d~z~* = 0.25 would not have matched in any case, because neither is consistent with a *t*-value of 18.04 (the [StatCheck](mod-stat-check.qmd) and [Effect Sizes](mod-stat-effect-size.qmd) modules flag both from the text alone).
- **The correlation**, *r* = 0.37, is reported, but no line of the code computes it.
- **The comparison between the years**, *t*(120.37) = -0.42, *p* = .673, has exactly the numbers the good paper reports, so it is probably correct. But the code stopped with an error before it reached this test, so it cannot be verified from what the authors shared.

The three *p*-values about accuracy (*p* = .07, *p* = .34, and *p* = .000) are not in the table at all. The module only checks a *p*-value that is reported together with its test statistic. Had they been checked, they would not have been found either: the repository contains no accuracy data.

## What it checks

Where [code_check](mod-code-check.qmd) asks *"is this code written well?"*, `reproducibility_check` asks a harder question: **could this code actually be run on this data — and do the numbers it produces match the ones the paper reports?** It is the module that stands closest to the goal of computational reproducibility.

The module works in two phases, and you choose how far to go:

1. A **static phase** (always run) that works out everything a reproduction attempt *would* involve — the dependencies, the file-path rewrites, the run order, the missing inputs — and reports where that attempt is likely to break, **without running any code**.
2. An **execution phase** (opt-in, `execute = TRUE`) that actually **runs the code**, either in a subprocess on your own machine or inside a locked-down Docker container, against a throwaway copy of the data, captures the statistical output it produces, and — together with any self-contained JASP/jamovi files in the deposit — lets you check whether the reported results are reproduced.

Both phases cover R code and Python code. Most of this chapter describes R; [Python code](#python-code) below describes where Python is handled differently.

::: callout-note
This module builds on `code_check`, `psychds_check`, and `data_check`, and inherits their **live network calls** to retrieve the repository files. You need an internet connection to run the code below.
:::

## The static phase, without running code

The default is the static phase — it does not run anything. This example reads every repository `demopaper()` links to, so (like the rest of this chapter) it needs those repositories to be reachable; the output below is shown rather than run live, so the chapter does not depend on every linked repository's uptime at render time:

```{r}
#| eval: false
paper <- demopaper()
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check")
mo$traffic_light
#> [1] "yellow"
cat(mo$summary_text)
#>
#> -  We assessed 6 R code files for reproducibility (static analysis; no code was run).
#> -  3 files appear runnable so far (parses, inputs resolve, placeable in the run order).
#> -  25 files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
#> -  2 referenced inputs unavailable (0 withheld due to size).
#> -  6 installable dependencies detected.
```

The `table` has one row per R or Python code file, carrying the static assessments as columns (there is no language column; the file extension shows the language):

```{r}
#| eval: false
mo$table[, c("file_name", "parses", "run_order", "order_basis",
             "paths_rewritten", "runnable")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

|               |file_name      |parses | run_order|order_basis | paths_rewritten|runnable |
|:--------------|:--------------|:------|---------:|:-----------|---------------:|:--------|
|test_script.R  |test_script.R  |TRUE   |         5|none        |               0|FALSE    |
|bad.R          |bad.R          |TRUE   |         2|none        |               0|FALSE    |
|bad.Rmd        |bad.Rmd        |TRUE   |         3|none        |               1|FALSE    |
|01.R           |01.R           |TRUE   |         1|numeric     |               0|TRUE     |
|good-example.R |good-example.R |TRUE   |         4|none        |               1|TRUE     |
|utils.R        |utils.R        |TRUE   |         6|none        |               0|TRUE     |

A file is marked `runnable` only when it parses, all of its referenced inputs resolve (they are present, or produced by an earlier script), and it can be placed in the run order. That is a deliberately strict bar for a *static* check: `runnable = FALSE` does not mean the code is broken, it means the module could not confirm, without running it, that everything the script needs is in place. When it *is* `FALSE`, the column `not_runnable_reason` names exactly why — one of `parse_error`, `unplaceable`, or `missing_input`, checked in that priority order — and `unresolved_inputs` names the specific file(s) that could not be resolved. Two further reasons apply only to an R file that does not parse as R: `not_r_content` when its content is not R at all (for example a JSON or HTML file saved with a `.R` extension), and `jags_model` when it is a JAGS/BUGS model definition. Neither counts as a parse error, because the file is not broken R code, and neither is run.

Two further list-columns, `reads` and `writes`, carry the basenames each script reads and writes (as `repro_file_io()` extracted them) directly on the table — useful if you want the code↔data provenance for a file without recomputing it yourself:

```{r}
#| eval: false
mo$table$reads
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "file.csv"
#>
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "example.csv"
#>
#> [[3]]
#> [1] "example.csv"  "example2.csv"
#>
#> [[4]]
#> character(0)
#>
#> [[5]]
#> [1] "file.txt"
#>
#> [[6]]
#> character(0)
mo$table$writes
#> [[1]]
#> character(0)
#>
#> [[2]]
#> character(0)
#>
#> [[3]]
#> character(0)
#>
#> [[4]]
#> character(0)
#>
#> [[5]]
#> character(0)
#>
#> [[6]]
#> character(0)
```

## Worked example: building a small reproducible fixture

To see every static assessment concretely, it helps to build a tiny, self-contained example rather than rely on whatever a real deposit happens to contain. The example below creates two scripts — one that writes an intermediate file, one that reads it back — and a plan that tells the module where a Psych-DS release would put the data.

```{r}
tmp <- withr::local_tempdir()

writeLines(c(
  'dat <- read.csv("data.csv")',
  'summ <- data.frame(mean_x = mean(dat$x))',
  'write.csv(summ, "intermediate.csv", row.names = FALSE)'
), file.path(tmp, "0_prep.R"))

writeLines(c(
  'summ <- read.csv("intermediate.csv")',
  'print(summ$mean_x)'
), file.path(tmp, "1_analysis.R"))

writeLines("x,g\n1,a\n2,a\n3,b\n4,b", file.path(tmp, "data.csv"))
```

The rest of the chapter uses these two files, `0_prep.R` and `1_analysis.R`, to demonstrate each static assessment on its own terms.

## The static assessments, function by function

Each static assessment is an exported helper, so you can run it on your own code independently of the module.

### Dependencies: `repro_dependencies()`

`repro_dependencies()` walks R code and returns the distinct packages it loads, tagged with **where each would be installed from** — a distinction `code_check`'s package list does not make. A `library()` call resolves to CRAN by default; a `remotes::install_github("user/repo")` call sets the install source of the package the code loads under that repository's name (with the pinned `@ref` kept when present); packages that ship with R are tagged `base`, because a run never needs to install them; and a bundled list of common **Bioconductor** package names (`edgeR`, `DESeq2`, and similar) is checked so those are tagged `bioc` instead of `cran` — confirmed as the single largest identifiable cause of install failures in a real corpus run, since a Bioconductor-only package is never on CRAN and `install.packages()` simply fails for it unless this distinction is made upfront.

```{r}
code_text <- c(
  "library(dplyr)",
  "library(ggplot2)",
  "remotes::install_github('tidyverse/ggplot2@v3.4.0')",
  "x <- stats::sd(1:10)"
)
repro_dependencies(code_text)
```

Note that a namespace-qualified call — `stats::sd(...)` and `remotes::install_github(...)` above — is picked up as a dependency even without an explicit `library()` call; the last row shows `stats` tagged `base`. `repro_dependencies()` also accepts a **list** of per-file character vectors and pools them into one result: when the same package is named both bare (`library(pkg)`) and via an explicit GitHub source somewhere else in the pooled files, the GitHub row wins, since it carries the real install source.

For R code, the dependency list is deliberately **name-only, not version-pinned**: static analysis cannot recover which version of a package was used. (Python code is the exception: see [Python code](#python-code) for how versions are read from a `requirements.txt` or `pyproject.toml`.) This is not a limitation to apologise for — it is the point. A reproduction runs against the *current* versions of these packages, and if it breaks under current versions, that break is itself a finding: it argues that the authors should have pinned their versions.

That said, `reproducibility_check` does not have to guess blindly at what "current" means. As of the version documented in this chapter, [code_check](mod-code-check.qmd) itself checks whether a deposit **declared** its environment at all — see [Declared R versions](#declared-r-versions-and-why-they-matter-for-docker) below, which explains how this feeds directly into the Docker execution path.

### Paths: `repro_rewrite_paths()` {#paths}

A script reads and writes data by relative path — `read_csv("raw/x.csv")`, `saveRDS(m, "../out/model.rds")`. When the release is re-laid-out into the Psych-DS structure, with data under `data/` and per-study `study-<group>/data/` folders, those paths no longer resolve. `repro_rewrite_paths()` maps each referenced path to its new location, using the file plan that [psychds_check](mod-psychds-check.qmd) produces.

Matching is by **basename**: a script's `../data/x.csv` and the repository's `raw/x.csv` are the same file seen from different working directories, so the prefix is ignored. When several files share a basename — a `demographics.csv` in more than one study — the ambiguity is resolved by **study group**: the candidate whose target path is in the same study as the script wins. Only when that still leaves more than one candidate is the reference left unrewritten and flagged as ambiguous, rather than guessed.

```{r}
plan <- data.frame(
  file_name = c("demographics.csv", "scores.csv"),
  target_path = c("study-ex1/data/source-demographics_data.csv",
                  "study-ex1/data/source-scores_data.csv"),
  current_path = c("ex1/demographics.csv", "ex1/scores.csv")
)
repro_rewrite_paths('d <- read.csv("data/demographics.csv")',
                    "ex1/analysis.R", plan)
```

Two refinements worth knowing about if you inspect this output closely:

- **Genuinely identical plan rows are not treated as ambiguous.** If the same physical file is listed more than once in the plan (which happens when a paper links several mirrored repositories), and every candidate row resolves to the *same* target path, that is not ambiguity — there was only ever one possible answer, and `repro_rewrite_paths()` recognises this rather than flagging it.
- **Mirror duplicates are collapsed by content, not by name**, when you pass `structure_df` (the `data_check` structure table). A paper linking an OSF component and its own "Archive of OSF Storage" snapshot can have the *same* physical file grouped into two different (and mostly wrong) study labels by upstream heuristics; `repro_rewrite_paths()` hashes each candidate's actual bytes first, so byte-identical mirrors count as one candidate rather than several conflicting ones.

### Run order: `repro_file_io()` and `repro_run_order()`

Scripts in a repository usually depend on each other, and running them in the wrong order fails for reasons that have nothing to do with reproducibility. `repro_file_io()` first extracts, for every file, the data it **reads**, the data it **writes**, and the scripts it **sources**:

```{r}
code_text_list <- list(
  "0_prep.R"    = readLines(file.path(tmp, "0_prep.R")),
  "1_analysis.R" = readLines(file.path(tmp, "1_analysis.R"))
)
io <- repro_file_io(code_text_list)
io
```

`repro_run_order()` then derives an order from three signals, in decreasing strength:

1. **read-after-write** — if one script writes `intermediate.csv` and another reads it, the writer must run first (a hard data dependency);
2. **`source()` edges** — if A `source()`s B, B must run first;
3. **numeric filename prefixes** — `0_prep.R` before `1_analysis.R`, and also embedded numbering such as `Exp1_02_...` before `Exp2_1_...` (a weak tie-breaker, not a dependency). The numeric key is the *vector* of every digit run anywhere in the filename, not just a leading prefix, so `Exp1_02_preprocessing.R` correctly sorts before `Exp2_1_import.R`.

Python has no equivalent of `source()` that the module follows, so Python scripts are ordered by the first and third signals only. For R, `repro_run_order()` also returns every `source()` link it found, as a data frame in its `"source_edges"` attribute (`from` is the script that is sourced, `to` the script that sources it); when the code is run, the module uses it to run a sourced script only inside the script that sources it (see the outcome `run_by_source` below).

The scripts are then topologically sorted. A dependency **cycle** (A reads a file B writes, and vice versa) cannot be ordered and is reported; so is an **ambiguous** ordering, where nothing — no dependency and no numbering — distinguishes the order of two or more files.

```{r}
repro_run_order(io)
```

`0_prep.R` runs first even though its own name sorts it that way anyway — but critically, the `order_basis` column reads `"dependency"`, not `"numeric"`, because the *real* reason is the data dependency: `1_analysis.R` reads `intermediate.csv`, which `0_prep.R` writes. `order_basis` is recorded on the file that has the **incoming** edge (the dependent file), not the file it depends on — so it is `1_analysis.R`'s row that carries `"dependency"` and names `0_prep.R` in `depends_on`.

### Missing inputs: `repro_missing_inputs()`

When a script reads a file that is not present, the reason matters. `repro_missing_inputs()` cross-references each unresolved read against the file plan and the download records, and classifies it as one of:

- `withheld_size` — the file *is* in the repository, but was not downloaded because it exceeded a size cap. This is a size-cap issue, not a reproducibility failure: raising `max_file_size` / `max_download_size` (in [data_check](mod-data-check.qmd)) would fetch it.
- `in_repo_not_downloaded` — listed in the repository but not present locally for another reason.
- `in_archive` — the file is in the repository only inside a `.zip` or `.tar` (for example `data.zip/data/x.csv`), and the code reads it at the path unpacking would give (`data/x.csv`). The reason reads "only inside data.zip; unpack it so the code finds it", and the script is not run.
- `absent` — not in the repository at all. The script reads a file the authors did not share (or that an earlier, un-captured step was meant to produce).

A file that a script writes itself, and then reads back, is not a missing input.

This distinction is the reason the static phase is worth running before a manual reproduction attempt: a run that fails because a 3 GB data file was skipped by the size gate is a completely different situation from a run that fails because the input data were never shared, and only the latter is a genuine openness problem.

### Two more static helpers you may not need directly

Two further exported helpers feed the module internally and are rarely called on their own, but are worth knowing about if you are extending the checks:

- **`repro_defined_vars(code_text_list)`** returns, for each R file, the variable names it assigns at its *top level* (not inside a function). This is what powers the corrective re-run for R described below: when a script fails with `object 'x' not found`, the module looks for exactly one other file whose `repro_defined_vars()` result includes `x`, and — if there is exactly one — infers that it must run first.
- **`repro_materialize_layout()`** and **`repro_write_scripts()`** build the throwaway Psych-DS-shaped directory the execution phase actually runs against, and write the path-rewritten scripts into it. You will see their effects described below (the `data/`, `output/`, and `statistical_output/` folders), but you would only call them directly if you were building your own execution pipeline on top of metacheck's static analysis. `repro_write_scripts()`'s `inject_libs` argument adds one or more `library()` calls to the top of a named R script; the corrective re-run uses it.

## Two ways to run the code {#two-ways-to-run-the-code}

Set `execute = TRUE` to actually run the paper's code. A second argument, `sandbox`, decides **where**:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# on this machine, in an isolated subprocess (the default)
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, sandbox = "process",
                 install_missing = TRUE, timeout = 600)

# inside a locked-down Docker container
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, sandbox = "docker",
                 install_missing = TRUE, timeout = 600)
```

The two options carry genuinely different risk, and the difference is worth understanding precisely rather than taking on faith:

| | `sandbox = "process"` (default) | `sandbox = "docker"` |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | a subprocess on your machine: a `callr` R process for an R script, a `python` process for a Python script | a `docker run` container |
| Isolates a crash? | Yes | Yes |
| Isolates the filesystem? | **No** — the code can read, write, or delete anywhere your R session can | **Yes** — `--read-only`, with only the throwaway sandbox directory writable |
| Isolates the network? | **No** — the code can reach the internet freely | **Yes** — `--network none` during the run phase |
| Runs as | your own user account | a fixed non-root user (uid 1000) inside the container |
| Requires | the `callr` package (only when the paper has R code); for Python code, the `processx` package and a Python interpreter (`python`, or else `python3`) | Docker installed and running, plus the `processx` package |
| Speed | fast — no container overhead | pre-built image (see below) makes this close to the process backend for most papers |

`sandbox = "docker"` achieves real containment with these `docker run` flags, applied to every script individually during the run phase:

```
--network none --read-only --tmpfs /tmp
--user 1000:1000 --cap-drop ALL
--security-opt no-new-privileges --pids-limit 512
-v <sandbox>:/sandbox -v <library>:/rlib:ro                       (R)
-v <sandbox>:/sandbox -v <library>:/pylib:ro -e PYTHONPATH=/pylib  (Python)
```

Network is fully disabled, the filesystem is read-only outside the mounted sandbox (with only `/tmp` and the sandbox itself writable), the container runs as a fixed non-root user, all Linux capabilities are dropped, privilege escalation is blocked, and the number of processes the container can spawn is capped. Before checking any of this, call `repro_docker_available()` to confirm Docker is installed and its daemon is actually running — `reproducibility_check()` calls this for you and stops with a clear message if it is not, rather than failing partway through a batch of papers with a cryptic error.

```{r}
#| eval: false
repro_docker_available()
#> $ok
#> [1] TRUE
#> $msg
#> [1] ""
```

::: callout-note
The dependency-install phase under `sandbox = "docker"` runs with the network **on** (it has to, to reach CRAN or GitHub, or for Python code the package index that `pip` installs from) but is otherwise hardened the same way — non-root, capabilities dropped, no new privileges. Only the per-script *run* phase disables the network entirely, since that is the phase running the paper's own, potentially untrusted, analysis code.
:::

::: callout-tip
Working through a whole corpus rather than one paper? [Batch mode](#batch-mode), described later in this chapter, runs several papers' `sandbox = "docker"` checks concurrently instead of one at a time.
:::

## The pre-built Docker image, and why it exists

The first time you think through what `sandbox = "docker"` needs to do to run a real paper's code, an obvious problem appears: most papers' scripts `library()` several packages that are not part of base R, and a container starts with nothing installed. Naively, every single `reproducibility_check()` call would need to install a paper's entire dependency list from scratch, inside a freshly-started container, before it could run a single script — for R packages with compiled C++ code (`rstan`, `lme4`, and dozens of others), that can mean minutes of compilation *per paper*.

To avoid that, Docker containers under `sandbox = "docker"` default to a **pre-built image**, `ghcr.io/scienceverse/metacheck_r_large:latest`, rather than a bare R installation. That image already has R, Quarto, JAGS, Java, the GDAL/GEOS/PROJ libraries for geographic data, and the roughly 750 most common packages a real corpus of psychology-science papers' code actually uses — found by scanning thousands of real `.R`/`.Rmd`/`.qmd` files for their `library()`/`require()` calls and pre-installing everything that showed up often enough to be worth the build cost. When a paper's dependencies are already in that list — which, for an ordinary `tidyverse`-and-`lme4`-shaped analysis, they usually are — the install phase does almost nothing, because `requireNamespace()` already finds the package. Only genuinely uncommon or paper-specific dependencies still need a real, from-source install. A smaller variant, `metacheck_r_small` (about 390 packages, each seen in at least three files of that scan, without the geographic libraries), is also published, but `reproducibility_check()` has no argument to choose it. Python code runs in a separate image, `ghcr.io/scienceverse/metacheck_py_small:latest` — see [Python code](#python-code).

The container's home folder cannot be written to, so R's cache, configuration and data folders are placed in `/tmp`. This lets a script run `renv::restore()`, which needs to write its cache. `rmarkdown::render()` finds the Pandoc program that Quarto bundles in the image, through the `RSTUDIO_PANDOC` environment variable.

The image, its Dockerfile, the full package list, and detailed notes on how it was built (including some genuinely non-obvious bugs found along the way — a package can report a successful install and still fail to *load*, because a runtime shared library it needs is missing from a minimal image) are all in a dedicated repository: [scienceverse/metacheck_docker_reproducibility](https://github.com/scienceverse/metacheck_docker_reproducibility). If you want to build your own variant — a smaller image with only the most common packages, or one that adds LaTeX for PDF rendering, or CmdStan for `cmdstanr`-based Bayesian models — that repository is the starting point, and its README documents exactly which levers actually reduce image size and which ones (surprisingly) do not.

## Declared R versions, and why they matter for Docker {#declared-r-versions-and-why-they-matter-for-docker}

This section applies to R code only; metacheck does not read a declared Python version, and Python code always runs in the pre-built Python image.

The pre-built image is fast, but it was built against one specific R version. A paper that deposited an `renv.lock` file, or a `sessionInfo()` text dump, or that pins its environment with `groundhog`/`checkpoint`, has told you *exactly* which R version its authors actually used — and that might not be the version the pre-built image happens to run.

[code_check](mod-code-check.qmd) is where this gets detected, as part of its own "Reproducible Environment" check: it looks for an `renv.lock` file anywhere in the repository (parsing its declared R version and every locked package + version), a `sessionInfo()`/`session_info()` dump (matched by filename — `sessionInfo.txt`, `session_info.txt`, and similar, or embedded in a README), or an actual `groundhog::groundhog.library()`/`checkpoint::checkpoint()` date-pin call in the code — a bare `library(groundhog)` with no pinning call does not count, since loading the package is not evidence anything was actually pinned.

```{r}
#| eval: false
cc <- module_run(paper, "code_check")
cc$traffic_light
#> [1] "yellow"
```

When nothing was declared, `code_check`'s own report explicitly says so and recommends depositing one — this is itself a piece of reproducibility hygiene worth checking regardless of whether you ever run the code.

`reproducibility_check()` has a parameter, `docker_use_declared_version`, that decides what to do with this information:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# default: always use the fast pre-built image, regardless of what the
# paper declared
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, sandbox = "docker")

# opt in to matching the paper's own declared R version exactly
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, sandbox = "docker",
                 docker_use_declared_version = TRUE)
```

By default (`docker_use_declared_version = FALSE`), the module always uses the pre-built `metacheck_r_large` image, prioritising speed. If the paper *did* declare a version, you get a warning naming the mismatch and explaining how to opt out of it — this is a deliberate design choice: silently running a paper's code against a different R version than the one its authors used could, in principle, change results, and that substitution should never happen invisibly.

```
Warning message:
reproducibility_check(sandbox = "docker"): this paper declared R version
4.3.1, but docker_use_declared_version = FALSE (the default), so the run
uses the pre-built metacheck_r_large image's own R version instead, for speed.
Set docker_use_declared_version = TRUE to match the paper's declared
version exactly -- slower, since every dependency then installs from
scratch rather than using the pre-built image.
```

Setting `docker_use_declared_version = TRUE` switches to a bare `rocker/r-ver:<declared version>` image with nothing pre-installed — genuinely slower, since every dependency now installs from source, but it matches the paper's own environment exactly. When a paper declared *no* version at all, this option falls back to bare `rocker/r-ver:latest` rather than silently reusing the pre-built image either — if you explicitly asked for version-matching, getting the fast pre-built image back through the back door when there was nothing to match against would defeat the point of asking.

## Checking many papers at once: batch mode {#batch-mode}

Everything so far runs one paper through `reproducibility_check()` at a time. If you are working through a whole corpus — a `paperlist` of dozens or hundreds of papers — calling it once per paper in a loop means only one Docker container is ever running: paper 2 does not start until paper 1's containers (install, then run) have both finished. For `sandbox = "docker"`, where each paper's own work is a slow, external `docker run` rather than in-memory R computation, that is time left on the table on any machine with more than one CPU core to spare.

Passing a `paperlist` together with `workers > 1` (and `execute = TRUE, sandbox = "docker"`) switches to **batch mode**: up to `workers` papers run their Docker checks at the same time, and the moment one paper finishes, the next paper in the list starts — never fewer than `workers` running while papers remain queued, never more.

```{r}
#| eval: false
papers <- papers_load("psychsci", cache = TRUE)[1:20]

mo <- module_run(papers, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, sandbox = "docker",
                 workers = 4, timeout = 600,
                 results_dir = "repro_results")
```

A few things are worth understanding about how this actually runs, rather than treating it as a black box:

- **Each paper runs in its own background R process** (via the `callr` package — install it if it is not already present), not in your current R session. This is deliberate, not an implementation detail you can ignore: `reproducibility_check()` reads and restores a few process-wide settings during a single-paper call (`llm_use()`, an internal option `data_check`/`code_check` share for API-limit handling), and those are not safe for several papers to set and restore *concurrently* in one shared session. A separate OS process per paper sidesteps the problem entirely — one paper's settings can never be observed by another's. Every `metacheck.*` option you have set in your own session (for example the cache directory) is copied into each background process, so each paper's run uses the same settings yours would.
- **Every other argument still means exactly what it means for one paper.** `timeout`, `install_missing`, `docker_use_declared_version`, `cache`, and everything else in [Options](#options) apply individually to each paper's own run; `workers` only controls how many of those individual runs are in flight together.
- **Container resource limits scale with `workers` automatically.** Each container is capped at `1/workers` of the host's CPU and memory (`--cpus`, `--memory`, in addition to the `--pids-limit 512` every container already had) — so four concurrent papers cannot collectively claim more than the whole machine, and one runaway script cannot starve the other three. You do not set this yourself; it is computed from `workers` and the host's own detected CPU count and RAM.
- **`results_dir` writes each paper's full result to disk as soon as that paper finishes** — one `<paper_id>.rds` file per paper, in the same format `capture_module_tables()` uses elsewhere in Metacheck for a corpus build. This matters for a batch that might take hours: if it is interrupted partway through (a crash, a machine restart, you stopping it deliberately), every paper that had already finished is safely on disk, not lost along with the ones still running. Read them back with `metacheck:::collect_module_tables("repro_results", "reproducibility_check")` — both `capture_module_tables()` and `collect_module_tables()` are internal helpers, not exported, so they need the `metacheck:::` prefix rather than a plain call.

```{r}
#| eval: false
mo$summary_table[, c("paper_id", "repro_ran_ok", "repro_deps")] |> head()
mo$summary_text
#> Ran the reproducibility check on 20 papers (up to 4 at a time): 17 ok, 2 red, 1 error.
```

The returned object has the same shape as a single-paper call, just with one row per paper in `$table` and `$summary_table` (tagged by `paper_id`, exactly like every other module that accepts a `paperlist`), plus one extra element: `$per_paper`, a named list holding each paper's own complete, untruncated module result — the full `$run_results`, `$install_results`, `$stat_output`, and `$report` you would get from calling `reproducibility_check()` on that paper alone.

::: callout-note
Batch mode is specific to `sandbox = "docker"`. Passing `workers > 1` with `sandbox = "process"`, with `execute = FALSE`, or with a single paper does nothing different — those paths are already fast enough, or already isolate only at the crash level rather than the process level, that running several at once is not worth the added complexity of a background-process pool. `workers` is simply ignored in those cases rather than raising an error, so a script that loops over papers with mixed settings does not need to branch on it itself.
:::

## Running the code: what happens during execution

Whichever `sandbox` you choose, the mechanics are the same:

1. **lays out the files** in a throwaway temporary directory (see [Two layouts](#two-layouts) below), so the run never touches your real archive or the download cache;
2. **writes the path-rewritten scripts** into that layout, so their reads and writes resolve;
3. optionally **installs the declared dependencies** into a throwaway library (`install_missing = TRUE`), never your main R library — under `sandbox = "docker"` this is *always* into a throwaway library inside the container, since a container has no access to your host library at all (Python packages are installed with `pip install --target` into a throwaway folder in the same way);
4. **runs each script in run order**, each in its own subprocess or container with a per-script `timeout`, capturing the outcome and the console output. An R script that another script runs with `source()` is not run on its own, but only as part of the script that sources it, and the same holds for a Python file that other files import.

```{r}
#| eval: false
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, install_missing = TRUE,
                 timeout = 600, keep_sandbox = TRUE)
```

### Two layouts {#two-layouts}

The `layout` argument sets which files the code runs against:

- **`"package"`** copies every file the run has (every file of a local folder; for a repository, every file that was downloaded, see `download`) to its own path, so a path that works in the package works in the sandbox. Only a path that cannot work as written is rewritten: an absolute path on the author's computer or a path out of the package, to the file with that name, and a path that counts from the script's own folder (`source("helpers.R")`, `"../data/x.csv"`) or from its RStudio project's (`.Rproj`) folder, to the file's path from the top of the package. This also applies to files the code makes: a script in `Study 2/` writing `"Data/processed.csv"` writes into `Study 2/Data/`. Any other relative path is left as written, also when other files share its name, since code commonly joins it with a folder of its own. A script's writes stay where the code puts them, so a later script reads the file where it expects it (only a write to an absolute path or out of the package goes to `output/`), and the copied files are writable, so a script can save over a file the package holds.
- **`"psychds"`** copies only the data files the module recognised, renamed and placed as a Psych-DS release, and rewrites the code's paths to match (see [Paths](#paths)). That suits a study whose scripts read a few tables, but code that reads folders of images or scan files, or imports its own helper modules from a subfolder, fails there for files that are in the package.
- **`"auto"`** (the default) uses `"package"` for a local folder (`local_path`, as `report_repository()` and the repository apps give it) and `"psychds"` otherwise.

```{r}
#| eval: false
module_run(NULL, "reproducibility_check", local_path = "path/to/folder",
           execute = TRUE, layout = "package")
```

### Time limits

`timeout` limits each script (600 seconds by default). `total_timeout` limits all scripts together, R and Python: by default one hour (3600 seconds), counted from when the first script starts. Use `NULL` or `Inf` for no limit, or give a clock time (`POSIXct`) by which all scripts must be done, such as a server's job limit minus the time its report needs. Once the time has run out, a running script is stopped and no further script is started, so a package with many slow scripts still gets a report. A script that was not started gets the outcome `skipped_time_limit`, which the report names, and the light is then at least yellow. A script the corrective second run (see below) has no time for keeps its first result.

To find the statistical results in what a script printed, the module searches only the first 20,000 lines of each script's printed output, and the report says when it stopped there. The search reads about 700 lines a second, so a script that prints a growing table in a loop could otherwise take longer to search than to run. Set another number with `options(metacheck.repro_output_max_lines = ...)`.

### Outcomes

Each script gets one of nine outcomes, added to the `$table` in an `outcome` column:

| Outcome | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ran_ok` | the script ran to completion without error |
| `errored` | the script raised an error (captured, with the message and output) |
| `timed_out` | still running at the `timeout` cutoff — **not** a failure, just slow; raise `timeout` for legitimately long analyses (e.g. Bayesian sampling) |
| `skipped_missing_inputs` | not run, because an input it needs is unavailable |
| `not_parsed` | not run, because the script does not parse (for Python, checked with Python's own parser; code written for Python 2 fails this check) |
| `dependency_unavailable` | not run (or failed immediately), because a package the script needs is missing: with `install_missing = TRUE`, it could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, *or* a named GitHub/URL source; with `install_missing = FALSE`, it is simply not installed on the computer or in the container that ran the script. Either way this is a limitation of where the code ran, not a defect in the paper's code. For Python: the script stopped with `No module named ...` for a package `pip` could not install, or that was not installed |
| `run_by_source` | an R script that another script runs with `source()`. It is run only inside that script, because on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first; its result is part of that script's result. A sourced script that does not parse or lacks an input keeps its own outcome instead |
| `run_by_import` | a Python file that other files import, such as `utils/data_handling.py`: a module that defines functions for the scripts that import it, which fails or does nothing on its own. It is not run, and not counted among the scripts that ran. A file with an `if __name__ == "__main__":` block still runs |
| `skipped_time_limit` | not run, because `total_timeout` had run out (see [Time limits](#time-limits)) |

`dependency_unavailable` is deliberately **excluded** from forcing the traffic light red, unlike `errored`/`timed_out` — a package that has genuinely vanished from every source metacheck tries is not evidence the paper's own analysis is broken.

Two R errors lead to one corrective re-run. An error whose message is `object '...' not found` usually means the script expects a variable another script defines. When exactly one other script in the repository defines that variable — checked via `repro_defined_vars()` — the module places that script first (adding a "definer runs first" edge and re-sorting). An error whose message is `could not find function "..."`, for a function no script of the paper defines, usually means a package was never loaded. The module then adds `library()` calls to the top of the failing script: all the packages the project's other scripts load, when one of them provides the function (such a script was usually written to run after those scripts, in the same R session); otherwise the one package, among the paper's own dependencies and a short list of very common packages, that exports the function; otherwise, for `%>%`, magrittr. Each added call is recorded in `$modifications`, and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after adding `library()` calls it should make itself. The module re-runs **once** and reports the corrected outcome. It does not iterate further: a second such error after that one corrective pass is accepted as the final result rather than chased indefinitely.

Python scripts get no corrective re-run; see [Python code](#python-code).

::: callout-note
Two habits in shared code are handled automatically. A `setwd()` call in R, or an `os.chdir()` call in Python — which hardcodes where the code must run and would override the sandbox — is replaced before the script runs by a statement that does nothing (`invisible(NULL)` in R, `pass` in Python), with the original call kept in a comment beside it, so a block that held only that call still has a statement. This also applies to `base::setwd()` and to `chdir()` under any module name (`from os import chdir`, or `o.chdir()` after `import os as o`). Each change is recorded in `$modifications`, and the report notes that the script is "reproducible after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code" (or an `os.chdir()`). An SPSS data file (`.sav`/`.zsav`/`.por`) with **no** accompanying syntax (`.sps`) turns the light red, because that analysis cannot be reproduced from the deposit; the same is true for a Stata `.dta` file with no `.do`. This holds whatever language the paper's code is in, also when the paper has only Python code. The report recommends depositing analyses as jamovi or JASP files instead, since those bundle data and analyses together and need no code to be re-run at all.
:::

::: callout-note
Byte-identical duplicate files are only run once. A paper that links several repository components mirroring the same materials — a "live" OSF component, an "Archive of OSF Storage" snapshot, a view-only anonymised link — would otherwise have `code_check` list the *same* script once per mirror, and the module would run it two, four, or more times for no reason. `reproducibility_check` hashes each resolved script's actual content and drops exact duplicates before running, naming which kept file each dropped one mirrors in the report.
:::

## Python code {#python-code}

Python code goes through the same two phases as R code, and the report describes it in its own section, headed "Python code", after the R sections. A `.py` file is Python code, and so is a Jupyter notebook (`.ipynb`) or Quarto document (`.qmd`) whose code is Python (`code_check` reads a notebook's declared kernel, and a Quarto document's declared engine or else its first code chunk). The code in a notebook or Quarto document is taken out of it first, so that `python` runs the code and not the notebook's JSON text or the document's Markdown.

The static phase differs from R in three ways:

- **Syntax check.** Each file is read by Python's own parser, which checks the syntax without running the code. This needs a Python interpreter (`python`, or else `python3`) on your computer; without one, every file is counted as parsing and the report says that the check could not be done. Code written for Python 2 (for example `print "x"`) fails this check.
- **Dependencies.** `repro_dependencies_py()` reads the packages from the `import` lines. Modules of Python's standard library are tagged `base`, the rest `pypi`. When the name a package is imported under differs from the name `pip` installs, the `pip` name is reported: `sklearn` becomes `scikit-learn`, `cv2` becomes `opencv-python`, `PIL` becomes `Pillow`, `yaml` becomes `PyYAML`, `bs4` becomes `beautifulsoup4`, and so on for about twenty such names. Unlike for R, versions can be known: when the repository has a `requirements.txt` (or, if not, a `pyproject.toml`), the requirement it states for a package is kept in `ref` and used when installing it.
- **Run order.** Python scripts are ordered by read-after-write and by the numbers in their filenames only.

```{r}
code_text <- c(
  "import numpy as np",
  "from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression",
  "import os"
)
repro_dependencies_py(code_text, manifest_text = "scikit-learn==1.3.0")
```

With `execute = TRUE`:

- Each Python script runs whole, as its own `python` process. With `sandbox = "process"` this needs the `processx` package and a Python interpreter on your computer; if no interpreter is found, or installing or running stops with an error, the Python files are reported as not run, with the reason, and the R results are still returned. With `sandbox = "docker"`, each script runs in its own container from the image `ghcr.io/scienceverse/metacheck_py_small:latest`, which has about 45 common packages (numpy, pandas, scipy, matplotlib, seaborn, scikit-learn, statsmodels, and others) already installed. `reproducibility_check()` has no argument to choose another Python image; only `repro_install_deps_py_docker()` and `repro_run_scripts_py_docker()`, called directly, take an `image` argument.
- With `install_missing = TRUE`, packages are installed with `pip install --target` into a throwaway folder, never into your own Python installation.
- Because each script runs in its own process, a name (a variable, function, or class) that one script defines is never available to another, whatever the order. A script that fails with a `NameError` is therefore not re-run; the report names the script or scripts that define the missing name instead.
- What a script prints is read with the same reader used for notebook outputs. A printed scipy result such as `TtestResult(statistic=4.89, pvalue=6.75e-05, df=22)` becomes a t-statistic, a p-value, and degrees of freedom, which are compared with the paper together with the R output (see [Matching the reported results against the output](#matching-the-reported-results-against-the-output)). Only the printed text is read: unlike for R, the result objects themselves are not recorded, so a value a script computes but never prints is not seen.

## What if there's no R or Python code at all?

Not every deposit has R or Python code to run, and the module handles several of those cases explicitly rather than falling through to a generic "nothing to check" result:

- **A JASP (`.jasp`) or jamovi (`.omv`) file, with no R or Python code anywhere** — these formats bundle the data *and* the analyses *and* the rendered results together, so they are reproducible from the file itself. The module still extracts and matches their statistics (see below); the traffic light is `yellow`, not `na`, because there is a real, substantive finding to report.
- **Stata `.do` files with a `.smcl` output log, but no separate `.dta`** — the `.smcl` log both recovers the executed syntax (as a synthetic `.do` file `code_check` can check) and carries the results it printed, extracted the same way as JASP/jamovi output.
- **Stata syntax with no data *and* no output at all** — named explicitly in the report as `"Stata code without data or output"`, with the light set to `info`, because this is real, actionable guidance (deposit a `.smcl` log) rather than an empty check.
- **The same for SPSS syntax with no data or output**, SAS code, MATLAB code, or any other language `code_check` recognises but this module does not execute: each gets its own named block explaining specifically what is missing, rather than one generic message.
- **Genuinely nothing at all** — no R or Python code, no self-contained output, no other-language code either — is the only case that returns `na`.

When a paper does have R or Python code, the same findings about SPSS/Stata files, self-reproducible output, and code in other languages are added to the report after the code sections (under the heading "All code and output" when there is Python code).

```{r}
#| eval: false
# a paper whose only "code" is a jamovi file
mo <- module_run(jamovi_only_paper, "reproducibility_check")
mo$traffic_light
#> [1] "yellow"
mo$summary_text
#> - We assessed 1 self-reproducible output file (JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/Mplus) instead of R code.
#> - 47 statistics stored from the extracted output.
```

## Extracting the statistical output

Running the code is only half of reproducibility — the other half is *the numbers it produces*. Several kinds of deposit already contain, or can be made to produce, a paper's statistical results, and the module extracts all of them into one common, structured form via `read_stat_tables()`:

- **JASP (`.jasp`) and jamovi (`.omv`) files** are self-contained: they bundle the data *and* the analyses *and* the rendered results. These are reproducible from the file itself — no code needs to run.
- **SPSS Viewer files (`.spv`)** likewise carry their own results structure, and — since the `.spv`'s own structure XML records the exact SPSS syntax that produced each table — the module also recovers that syntax as a synthetic `.sps` file, checked by `code_check` like any other syntax file.
- **Stata output logs (`.smcl`)** are Stata's own rendered output, echoing every command that was run; the module both extracts the printed results and recovers the commands as a synthetic `.do` file.
- **Mplus output (`.out`)** always self-documents: its own "INPUT INSTRUCTIONS" section holds the exact syntax that produced it, so there is no "data without syntax" failure mode for Mplus the way there is for SPSS and Stata.
- **Jupyter notebooks (`.ipynb`)** save each code cell's output *into* the file, so a Python analysis's printed statistics are recoverable with no Python installed and nothing re-run. (With `execute = TRUE`, the notebook's code is also run, as described in [Python code](#python-code).)
- **Python scripts**, when executed, have their printed output read the same way as a notebook's saved output.
- **R scripts**, when executed, print their results to the console (`summary(lm(...))`, `t.test(...)`, an `anova` table). The module parses that captured output into the same structured form, and — where possible — also captures the actual R **objects** a script's statements return (an `htest`, a `summary.lm`), not just their printed text, so a statistic's exact value and identity survive even when the console text alone would be ambiguous (the same `"W"` is Shapiro–Wilk's after `shapiro.test()` but the rank sum after `wilcox.test()`).

Every extracted statistic is typed with the **STATO** ontology (the *Statistical Methods Ontology*), so a `t`-value carries the accession for "t-statistic", a `p`-value the accession for "p-value", and so on; a statistic with no STATO class keeps its own column header as a plain label, so nothing is dropped.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# read the result tables out of a jamovi or JASP file directly
tables <- read_stat_tables("analysis.omv")
long   <- stat_results_long(tables, paper_id = "example",
                            source_file = "analysis.omv")
head(long[, c("source_file", "analysis", "statistic", "stato_label", "value")])
```

`stat_results_long()`'s full output has these columns: `paper_id`, `source_file`, `test_id`, `result_id`, `analysis`, `table_title`, `row_label`, `statistic`, `stato_label`, `stato_iri`, `value`, and `model_ref` (the last linking a captured statistic back to the fitted-model object it came from, when one exists — the same mechanism that makes `anova(m)` and `summary(m)$coefficients` findable as describing the same underlying model even though neither call names the other).

The full set of results for a paper is also written to a **structured JSON document** via `stat_output_json()` — one per source file, with a `schema`, `schema_version`, `paper_id`, `source_file`, `source_format`, and an `analyses` array of typed results. This is worth being precise about: it is a **metacheck-native schema**, not ISA-JSON. An earlier version of the module modelled this document on the ISA (Investigation/Study/Assay) vocabulary from the life sciences, but that forced statistical results into containers ("a t-test result as a Material") the vocabulary was never designed to hold — a repurposing metacheck itself invented, not an established convention. The current schema drops that borrowed vocabulary entirely in favour of a flat, self-describing document with a small set of named sections, in the spirit of formats like Psych-DS rather than conforming to an external schema that never quite fit.

## Matching the reported results against the output

The final question — the one reproducibility is really about — is whether the results **the paper reports** appear in the results **the analysis produces**. `match_reported_output()` answers it.

A reported statistical test is not a single number; it is a multi-component statement, for example *"M = 1.93, SD = 0.76, W = 183.5, p = .791, rb = -0.16"*. Metacheck's text extractor records each of those numbers in the paper's `$eq` table, grouped so that the numbers from one reported test stay together. `match_reported_output()` **recomposes** each reported test from its components, then checks whether those component values **co-occur in a single analysis of the extracted output**.

As the example at the start of this chapter showed, matching whole tests, rather than lone numbers, prevents a value from being found by coincidence.

Inside the module, this comparison is made once, after both the R and the Python code have run, so it uses the output of both languages together with any self-reproducible output. A printed scipy result names its values `statistic` and `pvalue`, which say nothing about the kind of test, so the kind is taken from the result's class name: `TtestResult` gives a t-statistic, `F_onewayResult` an F-statistic, `PearsonRResult` Pearson's r, and `Chi2ContingencyResult` a chi-squared statistic with its degrees of freedom (`dof`). `spearmanr()` and `kendalltau()` return the same class, so their coefficient is left without a type.

```{r}
#| eval: false
m <- match_reported_output(paper, mo$stat_output)
attr(m, "summary")
#> $n_tests   19
#> $n_found   14
#> $n_full    11   # every component of the test co-occurs in one analysis
#> $n_partial  3   # most components matched
#> $n_missing  5
```

Each row of the result is one recomposed reported test, with **where it was found**. The full column set is `text_id`, `grp_id`, `reported`, `n_components`, `n_matched`, `found` (logical), `match_values`, `not_matched`, `source_file`, `analysis`, `confidence` (`"full"`, `"partial"`, or `"none"`), and `plausible_split`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
m[m$found, c("reported", "n_matched", "confidence", "source_file", "analysis")]
#>                      reported n_matched confidence          source_file                 analysis
#>  M=1.93 SD=0.76 W=183.5 ...           5       full  experiment_1.omv   One Sample T-Test
#>  p=0.001 d=0.46                       2       full  across_all.omv     Paired Samples ...
```

So a reported test is not merely flagged as "found" — the module tells you **which deposited file and which analysis** produced the matching numbers, which is exactly the provenance a reader needs to trust that the paper's results are reproducible.

By default, `min_components = 1`, so even a **lone** reported statistic — a bare correlation coefficient with no accompanying test statistic — is checked. This is a change from an earlier version of the module, which defaulted to requiring at least two components before treating something as a matchable "test" at all; if you want that stricter behaviour, set `min_components = 2` explicitly.

`plausible_split` deserves a word of explanation, since it is easy to misread. Some reported values only match after being separated from the other values they were originally reported alongside — a mean split from its own confidence interval, say. `plausible_split` marks whether that separation is well-supported: `TRUE` when the split pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable via the output's own row labels, `FALSE` when no such link was found. A `FALSE` here is not necessarily wrong, but it is worth checking manually against the `source_file`/`analysis` columns before treating it as a confirmed match; `NA` means the value was never split in the first place, so the question does not apply.

If your extracted paper has any results tables (not just narrative text), pass `include_tables = TRUE` to also check statistics reported only in a table's cells against the extracted output.

## The traffic light and what you get back

| Light | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **green** | every script parses, its inputs resolve, the run order is unambiguous, no path rewrite is ambiguous, and (when executed) nothing errored |
| **yellow** | some obstacle short of a full reproduction failure — a parse error, an unresolved input, an ambiguous path or order, or a self-reproducible output file present with no R or Python code to run |
| **red** | a reproduction failure: code that errored or timed out when run, missing inputs that are *entirely* explained by size withholding, or SPSS/Stata data deposited without its syntax |
| **info** | no R or Python code and no self-contained output, but the module found something specific and actionable to say (e.g. Stata syntax with neither data nor an output log) |
| **na** | genuinely nothing to check — no R or Python code, no self-contained output, no other-language code either |

The static-only red condition is worth stating precisely, since it is easy to over-read: it fires when there **are** missing inputs and **every single one** of them is classified `withheld_size` — not merely when *some* inputs are size-withheld. Once code is actually executed (`execute = TRUE`), an execution error or timeout overrides the static signal and forces red regardless — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, whatever the static assessment said.

R code and Python code each get their own light by these rules, and the paper gets the more serious of the two (red before yellow before green). SPSS or Stata data without syntax then turns the paper's light red, whatever language its code is in.

| Element | What it contains |
|---|---|
| `$table` | one row per R or Python file: `parses`, `run_order`, `order_basis`, `depends_on`, `paths_rewritten`, `paths_ambiguous`, `setwd_removed` (for Python, the number of `os.chdir()` calls removed), `runnable`, `not_runnable_reason`, `unresolved_inputs`, `reads`, `writes`, and (when executed) `outcome`, `error_type`, `undefined_var` |
| `$summary_table` | per-paper aggregates (`repro_code_n`, `repro_runnable`, `repro_missing_inputs`, `repro_deps`, `repro_ran_ok`, `repro_tests_reported`, `repro_tests_matched`); the first five add up the R and the Python counts |
| `$run_results` | per-script execution record: `outcome`, `error`, `error_type`, `undefined_var`, captured `stdout` / `stderr`, `elapsed` time, `script_lines`, `captures` (the raw captured R objects; always empty for Python) |
| `$install_results` | per-dependency install record: `package`, `source`, `installed`, `message`, `via_archive`, `category` (for Python, always `FALSE` and `NA`) |
| `$stat_output` | per-file extracted statistical output: the structured JSON document and the flattened result rows |
| `$match_table` | the full `match_reported_output()` result, when there was output to match against |
| `$modifications` | per-file modification detail: `file_name`, `change_type`, `detail` — path rewrites (`path_rewrite`, listed even when `execute = FALSE`), and, when executed, `setwd()` or `os.chdir()` removal (`setwd_removed`), font substitution (`font_replaced`, R only), and added `library()` calls (`library_injected`, R only). Empty when nothing needed modifying |
| `$report` | formatted report sections, including per-script output and the self-reproducible JASP/jamovi results; the R sections come first, then a "Python code" section when there is Python code |
| `$summary_text` | plain-text bulleted summary, as one text also when the paper has R and Python code |
| `$checklist_section` | (only when `execute = TRUE`) the section the checklist report (`report_type = "checklist"`) shows for this check: how the scripts were run, what happened to each script in run order, other problems in the files, and how many of the paper's reported tests were found in the output of the code |
| `$brief` | `TRUE` when code was run and at least one script ran to the end, stopped with an error, or ran out of time; the brief report then keeps this check whatever its light |
| `$sandbox` | (only present when `keep_sandbox = TRUE`) the path to the materialised throwaway directory — see below |

## Options

| Argument | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `execute` | `FALSE` | run the paper's code; off by default |
| `sandbox` | `"process"` | `"process"` runs each R script in an isolated `callr` subprocess and each Python script in a `python` subprocess (isolates a crash only); `"docker"` runs inside a locked-down container (isolates filesystem and network too) |
| `docker_use_declared_version` | `FALSE` | when `sandbox = "docker"`, use the paper's own declared R version (slower, from-scratch install) instead of the fast pre-built `metacheck_r_large` image; R code only |
| `install_missing` | `FALSE` | install declared dependencies into a throwaway library before running (Python packages with `pip install --target`) |
| `cran_install_main` | `FALSE` | (only for R code, under `sandbox = "process"`) install CRAN-source dependencies into your real default library instead of a throwaway one, so they persist across papers in a batch run; ignored under `sandbox = "docker"`, where a container never has access to your host library |
| `layout` | `"auto"` | which files the code runs against: `"package"`, `"psychds"`, or `"auto"` (`"package"` for a local folder) — see [Two layouts](#two-layouts) |
| `timeout` | `600` | per-script timeout in seconds |
| `total_timeout` | `3600` | time for all scripts together, in seconds from when the first script starts, or a clock time (`POSIXct`); `NULL` or `Inf` for no limit — see [Time limits](#time-limits) |
| `keep_sandbox` | `FALSE` | keep the throwaway run directory and return its path as `$sandbox`, to inspect exactly what ran |
| `workers` | `1` | when `paper` is a paperlist and `sandbox = "docker"`, run this many papers' checks concurrently — see [Batch mode](#batch-mode) |
| `results_dir` | `NULL` | with `workers > 1`, write each paper's result to `<paper_id>.rds` in this directory as soon as that paper finishes |
| `local_path`, `local_only` | | `local_path` adds the files in a local folder; `local_only = TRUE` skips the online repository lookups. With a paper, `local_path` alone does not replace the repository the paper links to: that repository is still downloaded, and its scripts run alongside the local ones, so a local and an online version of the same script can both run. Give both to run only the local files |
| `model`, `params` | | passed through to the upstream modules' LLM calls (`data_check`, `psychds_check`), only used when `llm_use(TRUE)` |
| `cache` | `FALSE` | forwarded to the internal `data_check`/`code_check` runs: keep downloaded files in the persistent on-disk cache and reuse them on later runs |
| `download`, `skip_types`, `peek_zips`, `max_file_size`, `max_download_size` | (same as `data_check`'s own defaults) | forwarded to the internal `data_check` run — see the [Data Check](mod-data-check.qmd) chapter for what each one controls |
| `skip_on_api_limit` | `FALSE` | give up immediately on a confirmed API rate limit instead of waiting, forwarded to the internal repository/data/code checks |
| `tables_dir` | `NULL` | a directory of per-paper `.rds` files from a prior full corpus build (written by the internal `capture_module_tables()`); when set, a reproducibility-only re-run reads that paper's already-computed `data_check`/`code_check`/`psychds_check` results from disk instead of re-running them |

::: callout-warning
`download`, `skip_types`, and `peek_zips` are also part of the key the LLM response cache uses for `data_check`'s column classification — changing any of them between runs on the same paper produces a different file set and therefore a cache miss, even though the paper and the underlying question are identical.
:::

`keep_sandbox = TRUE` is worth using deliberately rather than as a debugging afterthought: the directory it preserves contains the files the code ran against (`data/` for the Psych-DS layout, or a copy of the whole package for the package layout), `output/` (anything a script's write calls were redirected into), and — whenever there is any extracted statistical output at all, whether from execution or from a self-contained JASP/jamovi/`.spv`/`.smcl`/`.out` file — a `statistical_output/` folder with the structured results documents. `convert_psychds()`, which is meant to put this folder into a Psych-DS archive, is not yet available in the released version or in `dev`; see the [Psych-DS Check](mod-psychds-check.qmd) chapter.

## Notes and limitations

Honest limits worth keeping in mind:

- The static phase cannot always tell that a file a script reads is an **intermediate produced by another script** under a different name, so it may report it as an "absent" input.
- Helper scripts `source()`d through a **dynamically built path** do not get a source edge, so they order arbitrarily with basis `none`.
- Only **R** and **Python** are executed. SPSS syntax, Stata syntax, SAS, and MATLAB are reported but not run; SPSS/Stata/JASP/jamovi/Mplus results are read from their own output files, and a notebook's saved results from the notebook, rather than recomputed.
- Each Python script runs in its own process, so a script written to run after another one in the same Python session fails on the names that other script defines; there is no corrective re-run for Python. Python dependencies come only from `import` lines, so a package imported under a name other than its `pip` name is installed correctly only when that name is in the module's built-in list.
- The output parser handles the common R output shapes (one-line tests like `t.test`; fixed-width tables like `summary(lm)` and `aov`), printed Python results such as scipy's, and JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/Mplus/notebook result tables. Unusual or bespoke output may parse incompletely; statistics with no STATO class are kept under their own header rather than semantically typed.
- Extracted values inherit the **display precision** the software reported (`p = "< .001"` is a threshold, `t = 2.77` is rounded), so matching is precision-aware rather than exact — it compares what was *reported*, which is what you want for a reproducibility check.
- `sandbox = "process"` genuinely does run downloaded code on your own machine with your own user's filesystem and network access. If you are not confident in a paper's code, use `sandbox = "docker"` instead — the two are not equivalent safety-wise, only equivalent in what they check.
- The pre-built R Docker image is built for one specific R version at a time; if a paper's own declared version matters to you specifically (not just "some recent R"), use `docker_use_declared_version = TRUE` and accept the slower, from-scratch install.

## Open for feedback

Making this software was a challenge. We have validated the code by running it on more than 3000 scientific papers, with hundreds of folders of data and code, across dozens of data repositories. But there will be bugs. Software this complex, that tries to process the almost infinite ways in which researchers can share data and code, is bound to run into bugs. When thousands of people try this out, for some it will fail on their very first try (while for many others, it will run fine). If you find a bug, please raise an issue on [Metacheck's GitHub page](https://github.com/scienceverse/metacheck/issues). You need to share the data or code files that lead to the problem with us, or we can't fix the problem. If you can't share the data and code, you can ask an AI agent to analyze the problem, which might be enough to solve it as well. If the tool lacks features you would like to have, let us know, and we will do our best to build them in.
